{{Short description|Italian physicist (1927–2014)}}
{{lead too short|date=October 2014}}
'''Emilio Picasso''' (9 July 1927, in [[Genoa]] – 12 October 2014) was an Italian [[physicist]].<ref>[http://www.pisatoday.it/cronaca/scomparsa-del-fisico-emilio-picasso-gia-direttore-della-scuola-normale-e-accademico-dei-lincei-il-cordoglio-del-sindaco-filippeschi.html Scomparsa del fisico Emilio Picasso] (in Italian)</ref> For most of his career, he served as a researcher at [[CERN]] and was project leader for the [[Large Electron–Positron Collider|Large Electron-Positron Collider]] (LEP), one of the largest [[particle accelerator]]s ever constructed. Picasso was awarded the [[Legion of Honour]] from France and is also bearer of the [[Order of Merit of the Italian Republic|Knight Grand Cross of the Italian Republic]], Italy's highest civilian honor.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sutton|first1=Christine|title=Emilio Picasso's contagious enthusiasm for physics|journal=CERN Courier|date=January 2015|volume=55|issue=1|pages=19–20|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1983144}}</ref> When he died, his hometown newspaper called it a moment of mourning for "the international scientific community and for Pisa."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gonews.it/2014/10/13/pisa-ci-lascia-il-fisico-emilio-picasso-fu-direttore-della-normale-e-accademico-dei-lincei/|title=Ci lascia il fisico Emilio Picasso. Fu direttore della Normale e accademico dei Lincei|date=2014-10-13|website=gonews.it|language=it-IT|access-date=2019-03-04}}</ref>

==Life and career==
Picasso studied first [[mathematics]] and then two years [[physics]] at the [[University of Genoa]]. After his [[doctorate]], he started working there as an assistance [[professor]] for [[experimental physics]]. At the beginning he kept himself busy with [[atom physics]], but then his interests changed to [[elementary particle physics]]. Therefore, he worked at the [[Betatron]] in [[Turin]] and then at the [[Synchrotron]] in [[Frascati]]. In the years 1961/62 he worked in a group led by [[Cecil Powell]], which researched [[cosmic rays]] with balloons.

Two years later in 1964 he joined [[CERN]] for researching the [[Landé g-factor|anomalous magnetic moment]] of [[muon]]s, which was a precision test for the [[quantum electrodynamics]]. The so-called [[Muon g-2#Muon g − 2 at CERN|''g minus 2'' experiment]] was an idea of [[Leon M. Lederman|Leon Lederman]]. Picasso worked in a collaboration with physicists John Bailey, [[Francis Farley]], [[Simon van der Meer]], [[Guido Petrucci]] and [[Frank Krienen]]. At this experiment a 10 [[Electronvolt|GeV]] [[Proton|beam of protons]] is ejected by the [[Proton Synchrotron]]. This beam is headed on target inside one of the Muon [[Storage ring]]s, which were built for this experiment. There 70% of the [[proton]]s interact with each other producing a burst of particles, among other things many negative [[pion]]s. The [[pion]]s, which have the right momentum (about 1,3 [[Electronvolt|GeV]]/[[Speed of light|c]]), turn in the [[Magnetism|magnetic field]] so that they can orbit the [[Storage ring|ring]]. There the pions decay rather quickly, in the first turn around one fifth of them change to negative [[muon]]s. Some of these muons which are emitted at small angles to the direction of the pions have slightly lower momentum than the pions and therefore move to an orbit of smaller radius. So they miss the target at the end of the first turn and are kept orbiting in the magnet ring. The measurement needed 15 years and at the end, they calculated the [[Landé g-factor|g-factor]] and the [[magnetic moment]]um of a muon.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Who ever ordered that?|journal=CERN Courier|date=August 1966|volume=6|issue=8|pages=152–155|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1728816?ln=en}}</ref>

After that Picasso was concerned with the design of a [[Superconductivity|superconducting]] [[gravitational-wave detector]]. In the year 1980 the [[List of Directors General of CERN|director-general]] [[Herwig Schopper]] announced him to be the project leader of the [[Large Electron–Positron Collider|LEP]] at the CERN.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Schopper |first1=Herwig |chapter=Director-General of CERN |date=2024 |title=Herwig Schopper: Scientist and Diplomat in a Changing World |pages=119–162 |editor-last=Schopper |editor-first=Herwig |series=Springer Biographies |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-031-51042-7_7 |isbn=978-3-031-51042-7 |last2=Gillies |first2=James |editor2-last=Gillies |editor2-first=James|doi-access=free }}</ref> Here he could use his knowledge about [[Superconductivity|superconductors]]. At the beginning they planned a bigger ring, which should go 12&nbsp;km under the [[Jura Mountains]]. But because of the high water pressure, the tunnel expert [[Giovanni Lombardi (engineer)|Giovanni Lombardi]] disadvised from this layer, so they reduced the way under the [[Jura Mountains]] and the collaboration transferred the ring. But also 3&nbsp;km under the mountains was difficult to build and "the mountains answered" (Picasso), water broke in and they had to reduce the length of the tunnel, because it was not possible to build under the [[Jura Mountains|mountains]]. At the 14 July 1989 the [[Large Electron–Positron Collider|LEP]] was brought on line like Picasso promised president [[Jacques Chirac]] two years ago.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Inside story: 'OK, I've finished my job now'|journal=CERN Courier|date=September 2009|volume=49|issue=7|page=42|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/1734422?ln=en}}</ref> In the year 1992, he resigned at CERN and became director at the ''[[Scuola Normale Superiore]]'' in [[Pisa]], where he continued in collaboration with the [[University of Genoa]] his researches about [[gravitational-wave detector]].

==Awards==
Picasso was a member of the ''[[Académie des sciences]]'' and the ''[[Accademia Nazionale delle Scienze]]''. Furthermore, he was bearer of the [[Legion of Honour]] and bearer of the [[Order of Merit of the Italian Republic|Knight Grand Cross of the Italian Republic]].
